h1: The 6 Best Mini-LED TVs of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: six Mini-LED TVs from TCL, Hisense and Roku, from 55 to 85 inches, sorted by refresh rate, size and who each one suits.
summary: The TCL 65 inch QM8K is the best Mini-LED TV here: a 65 inch QLED Mini-LED with 120Hz sized for most living rooms. The TCL QM8L adds 144Hz at 75 inches, and the Hisense U7 reaches 165Hz in both 85 and 55 inch sizes. The Roku Pro is the streaming-first pick.
intro: Mini-LED has become a sticker, and shoppers read it as a guarantee. The backlight idea is shared: thousands of tiny LEDs, grouped into dimming zones behind an LCD, so bright highlights and dark corners can coexist better than on an ordinary LED set. What differs between sets is everything around it, starting with refresh rate and the smart platform, and the listings give you little else to compare.

We reviewed eight listings, dropped a TCL entry whose spec line contradicted its own title, and ranked six on refresh rate, size, platform and price bucket. We read spec sheets and make no picture-test claims, so brightness and zone counts, which do the real work, stay unranked until you confirm them on the maker's page.

products.name: TCL 65 Inch Class QM8K Series
products.verdict: A 65 inch QLED Mini-LED at 120Hz sized for most living rooms.
products.description:
The QM8K is a 65 inch QLED Mini-LED TV with a 120Hz refresh rate, in the $500 and up bucket. Sixty-five inches is the size most living rooms are laid out around, and 120Hz is the smooth baseline for sports and console games: it keeps fast motion clearer than a standard 60Hz panel when action crosses the screen.

It takes first place because it fits the widest range of rooms while keeping the refresh rate where it matters. The QM8L reaches 144Hz, but it also asks for a bigger wall.

Buy it for a typical living room. The caveat is that the listing says little about brightness, and brightness is what separates Mini-LED sets in a sunlit room. Check detailed specs before buying, and skip it if you want 144Hz or higher.

products.name: TCL 75 Inch Class QM8L Series
products.verdict: A 75 inch set that steps up to 144Hz.
products.description:
The QM8L is a 75 inch QLED Mini-LED TV with 144Hz refresh, in the $500 and up bucket. A 144Hz panel pays off for PC gaming and fast console titles, where a higher refresh rate shortens the gap between a button press and the next frame.

It ranks second because the step from 120Hz to 144Hz is a niche gain, and the larger 75 inch panel needs space the QM8K does not. Compared with the Hisense U7, it is smaller than the 85 inch and slower than the 165Hz U7, so it sits between the two.

Buy it for a big wall and fast motion. The caveat is room size: a 75 inch set demands viewing distance and a sturdy stand. Skip it if your room is small, where the QM8K gives you nearly the same experience in a smaller body.

products.name: Hisense 85" U7 Mini-LED ULED 4K UHD Best Premium Gaming Smart Google
products.verdict: 85 inches and 165Hz for the biggest screen in the lineup.
products.description:
The Hisense U7 in 85 inches is a Mini-LED ULED 4K set with 165Hz refresh, running a Google smart platform, in the $500 and up bucket. It has the highest refresh rate in the ranking and the biggest screen, which together make it the cinema-and-gaming extreme.

It ranks third because sheer size suits few rooms. An 85 inch panel needs a lot of wall, and a strong mount or stand, and it must fit through your doors. It beats the TCLs on scale and refresh rate, but it asks the most from your room.

Choose it for a dedicated media room. Skip it if your wall is under about six feet wide, or if your seating is close to the screen. The Google platform brings familiar apps, and the listing otherwise gives few details on brightness or zones.
products.skipIf: Your wall is under 6 feet wide.

products.name: Hisense 55" U7 Mini-LED ULED 4K UHD Best Premium Gaming Google Smart
products.verdict: The same U7 line in 55 inches with 165Hz for smaller rooms.
products.description:
The 55 inch U7 carries a Mini-LED ULED 4K panel with 165Hz and a Google smart platform, in the $500 and up bucket. It is the same line as the 85 inch, scaled down to a bedroom or den, and it keeps the top refresh rate in the group.

It ranks fourth because it gives up the 85 inch model's size for a more flexible footprint. The 165Hz figure is the highest here, which helps PC and fast console games, though 55 inches is a small canvas for a premium Mini-LED price.

It suits a gaming bedroom or a desk-side setup. Skip it if you sit far from the screen, since 55 inches shrinks at distance. For a main living room, the TCL QM8K at 65 inches gives you more picture at the same bucket.
cons: Small screen for a living room
products.skipIf: You sit far from the screen.

products.name: Hisense 75" U6 Pro Series Mini‑LED ULED 4K UHD HDR Gaming AI Smart
products.verdict: A 75 inch 144Hz Hisense with HDR and AI smart features.
products.description:
The Hisense U6 Pro is a 75 inch Mini-LED ULED 4K set with 144Hz refresh, HDR and AI smart features. The listing shows no price bucket, which means you must check cost yourself.

It sits fifth because of that gap. Against the TCL QM8L, it matches the 144Hz and the 75 inch size, and it offers HDR in its listing, but the missing price makes it impossible to rank on value. Detail on brightness and zones is also thin.

It suits a big-screen shopper comparing Hisense and TCL. Skip it if you need confirmed pricing before deciding. If the live price lands below the QM8L, it becomes a more serious contender, since the specs line up closely. Verify HDR support and zone counts on the manufacturer page.

products.name: Roku 75-Inch Pro Series Smart TV - 4K QLED Mini-LED TV - RokuTV
products.verdict: A 75 inch 4K QLED Mini-LED with Roku's simple interface.
products.description:
The Roku 75 inch Pro Series is a 4K QLED Mini-LED TV running Roku's own platform, in the $500 and up bucket. Roku's strength is a simple home screen built around app tiles, which suits households where several people share the remote and nobody wants menus.

It ranks last because no refresh rate is listed, and refresh rate matters to anyone who plays fast games. The TCL and Hisense sets state theirs, from 120Hz to 165Hz, so this one asks you to trust the spec sheet blind.

Buy it for a streaming-first household that values simplicity over gaming speed. Skip it if you are a competitive gamer. Check the refresh rate on the live listing before ordering, and compare it against the QM8K if gaming matters even slightly.

whatMatters.detail: Refresh rate is how many times per second the screen updates. 120Hz suits sports and consoles, while 144 to 165Hz favors PC and fast games. Look for the Hz figure in the title or specs. A missing figure, as on the Roku Pro, is a reason to ask before buying, and a console owner should insist on seeing it.

A bigger panel is not always better. For 4K, sitting about 1.5 times the diagonal away is a common rule of thumb. Measure your viewing distance and wall width before choosing between 55, 65, 75 and 85 inches, and leave space for a stand or mount strong enough for the weight, which grows quickly with size.

Google, Roku and others differ in apps, menus and voice features. Pick the one your household finds easiest to use. Look for the platform name in the title, as on the Hisense U7's Google smart label and the Roku Pro. A platform you dislike will annoy you every day, whatever the panel does, so try the interface in a store if you can.

Mini-LED uses many small backlight zones, and QLED adds a quantum dot layer for color. The two terms describe different things and are often combined. Check that the listing names both, as the TCL QM8K does, and not just one marketing label that could hide a plain edge-lit panel, and do not assume every Mini-LED label means the same hardware.

Some listings omit brightness or zone counts, the two figures that matter most for Mini-LED. Look for them on the manufacturer page before buying, since a sheet that stays silent on them offers little to separate sets. Do not assume the backlight tech is the same across brands. Zone counts vary widely between models and price tiers.

faq.a: It is an LED backlight made of very small LEDs grouped into zones. More zones generally means finer control of brightness, so highlights glow without washing out dark areas nearby, which is the main reason to pay for the technology.

faq.q: Does Mini-LED burn in like OLED?
faq.a: Mini-LED uses an LED backlight, so it avoids the burn-in concerns tied to OLED, though listings do not guarantee this. Check each maker's warranty terms if static images such as game HUDs or news tickers worry you.

faq.q: Is a 165Hz TV worth it over 120Hz?
faq.a: Only for PC or high frame-rate gaming. Sports and movies look fine at 120Hz, so the TCL QM8K covers most households with room to spare. The Hisense U7 at 165Hz matters mainly if your graphics card can push those frames.

Buying the biggest size without measuring the viewing distance and the wall. An 85 inch Hisense U7 overwhelms most rooms, so match the panel to the seat, not to the price jump, and measure the wall before you order.

faq.q: How do I set one up?
faq.a: Connect to Wi-Fi, sign into your streaming accounts and turn on the game mode for consoles. Google and Roku platforms walk you through setup on first boot.

faq.q: Why was one TCL left out?
faq.a: The QM6K listing carried an OLED spec line that contradicted its Mini-LED title, so we dropped it. We would rather leave a set out than rank a contradictory spec sheet.

finalTake: Buy the TCL QM8K for a typical living room, or the QM8L when a larger wall and faster motion matter. Gamers who want 165Hz should look at the Hisense U7, in 55 or 85 inches. The Roku Pro suits streaming households that value a simple home screen. Verify brightness and zone counts before you pay.
